text: 1 · Classification at a threshold A binary classifier outputs a score; a threshold turns it into a decision, and the decisions against the truth fill the confusion matrix : true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN), false negatives (FN).
label: core

text: Every metric in this section is a ratio of those four counts at one threshold ( Google ML Crash Course ).
label: core

text: Metric Formula Reads as Accuracy (TP + TN) / all Share of decisions that were right Precision TP / (TP + FP) Of everything I flagged positive, how much was right Recall (true positive rate, sensitivity) TP / (TP + FN) Of all actual positives, how many I caught F1 2PR / (P + R) Harmonic mean of precision and recall F β (1 + β²)PR / (β²P + R) Recall counted β times as important as precision ( van Rijsbergen 1979 , chapter 7) False positive rate (FPR) FP / (FP + TN) Fraction of actual negatives wrongly flagged Specificity (true negative rate) TN / (TN + FP) 1 − FPR Balanced accuracy (recall + specificity) / 2 Accuracy with both classes weighted equally MCC (TP·TN − FP·FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)) Correlation between decision and truth, from −1 to 1, 0 for guessing ( Matthews 1975 ) F1 never looks at TN: it is the score of the class you act on.
label: depth

text: 2 · Ranking: ROC and precision-recall curves Sweeping the threshold from high to low traces two curves.
label: core

text: The ROC curve plots recall (TPR) against FPR; its area, ROC-AUC , equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored above a randomly chosen negative, with ties counted half ( Hanley and McNeil 1982 ; Fawcett 2006 ).
label: core

text: The precision-recall (PR) curve records precision and recall at each threshold, and its area is AUPRC .
label: core

text: A random ranker scores ROC-AUC 0.5 whatever the classes, but AUPRC equal to the share of positives, so the two areas are not on the same scale.
label: core
key: AUPRC equal to the share of positives

text: Why ROC misleads when positives are rare comes down to one denominator.
label: core

text: FPR divides by all negatives, which is a huge number, so even thousands of extra false positives barely move it while recall moves quickly; the ROC curve looks good regardless.
label: core

text: Precision divides by the model's own positive predictions, so it is hit by every one of those false positives ( Davis and Goadrich 2006 ).
label: core

text: Use AUPRC when positives are rare.
label: core
key: Use AUPRC, or precision at the recall you need

text: The root page's widget shows it with a fixed classifier as positives get rarer: ROC-AUC stays at 0.856 while AUPRC falls from 0.85 to 0.11 ( Topic: ml-fundamentals , Reading, step 7).

text: One curve dominates another in ROC space if and only if it dominates in PR space, so a ranking that is better everywhere is better on both.
label: core

text: But points in PR space cannot be joined by straight lines: precision does not interpolate linearly, so the trapezoidal area under a PR curve is optimistic.
label: core

text: That is why scikit-learn's average_precision_score sums precision times each step in recall with no interpolation; "AUPRC" in papers may be either, and the two differ.

text: 3 · Probabilities: calibration, log-loss and Brier Ranking metrics ignore what a score means.
label: core

text: A classifier is calibrated when, of all the examples it gives probability 0.8, about 80% are positive.
label: core
key: of all the examples it gives probability 0.8

text: Two scores measure probabilities directly.
label: fat

text: Log-loss is the cross entropy of the predicted probability of the true class, −mean log p (true class), which is the training loss read as a measurement.
label: core
key: the training loss read as a measurement

text: The Brier score is the mean squared error of the probability against the 0 or 1 outcome ( Brier 1950 ).
label: core

text: Both are proper scoring rules : the expected score is best when the forecast equals the true probability, so neither can be gamed by hedging ( Gneiting and Raftery 2007 ).
label: core

text: A reliability diagram bins predictions by confidence and plots the observed rate in each bin; the expected calibration error (ECE) is the sample-weighted mean gap between confidence and observed rate over the bins ( Guo et al.
label: core

text: 2017 , who found that modern deep networks, unlike those of a decade earlier, are poorly calibrated, and that temperature scaling, one parameter, fixes most of it).
label: core

text: ECE depends on the binning (here 10 equal-width bins) and is not a proper scoring rule.
label: core
key: is not a proper scoring rule

text: The more accurate model is the worse forecaster.
label: core
key: The more accurate model is the worse forecaster

text: A multinomial naive Bayes classifier on the same SST-2 features is slightly more accurate than the logistic regression ( against at threshold 0.5) and ranks almost as well, yet its probabilities are far worse: naive Bayes multiplies word evidence as if words were independent, which pushes its outputs towards 0 and 1 ( Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana 2005 ).
label: core

text: Isotonic regression, a monotone step function fitted on cross-validated predictions ( Zadrozny and Elkan 2002 ), maps them back towards observed frequencies without changing their order.
label: core

text: The animation runs the same 872 predictions before and after.
label: core
key: Same 872 predictions before and after isotonic calibration

text: Try: step through slowly.
label: fat

text: Accuracy and ROC-AUC barely move between the first and last step; log-loss halves. positive review negative review observed rate in bin perfect calibration Real predictions: multinomial naive Bayes (alpha 1, word and bigram counts) and the same model with 5-fold isotonic calibration ( CalibratedClassifierCV ), both trained on SST-2 train; logistic regression as above for reference.
label: core

text: Log-loss clips probabilities at 10 −15 , the default of older scikit-learn versions; with a 10 −6 clip naive Bayes scores 0.83 instead of 0.85.
label: core

text: Calibration is a separate axis from accuracy, so measure it whenever a probability is used as a probability: a risk threshold, an expected cost, an abstention rule, a confidence shown to a user, or a score fed to another model.
label: core

section: 5 · text against a reference: bleu, rouge, meteor, chrf
text: Metric Mechanism Origin, notes BLEU For n = 1 to 4, the share of the output's n -grams found in the reference, each clipped to the count the reference has ("modified precision"); their geometric mean, times a brevity penalty BP = exp(1 − r / c ) when the output length c is below the reference length r , else 1 Machine translation; precision-oriented; defined over a whole test corpus ( Papineni et al.
label: core

section: 5 · text against a reference: bleu, rouge, meteor, chrf
text: 2002 ) ROUGE-N Precision, recall and F1 of matching n -grams Summarisation; recall-oriented ( Lin 2004 ) ROUGE-L Longest common subsequence of the two word sequences, as precision, recall and F1 Order-sensitive without requiring contiguity ROUGE-S Skip-bigram co-occurrence: every ordered pair of words, any gap apart Allows gaps within bigrams; rarely reported now METEOR One-to-one unigram alignment in stages (exact words, then Porter stems, then WordNet synonyms); F mean = 10PR / (R + 9P); penalty 0.5 × (chunks / matches) 3 , where a chunk is a run of matches adjacent and in the same order in both; score = F mean × (1 − penalty) Built to score single sentences ( Banerjee and Lavie 2005 ) chrF Character 1- to 6-gram precision and recall (spaces removed), averaged over orders, combined as F β with β = 2 Robust to word forms and spelling ( Popović 2015 ) BLEU is a corpus metric: summed over a test set, a sentence with no 4-gram match does not zero the score.
label: core

section: 6 · perplexity, and why it depends on the tokenizer
text: 6 · Perplexity, and why it depends on the tokenizer Perplexity is the reciprocal geometric mean of the probabilities a model gives each token of a text: PPL = (∏ i p ( w i | w < i )) −1/ N = exp(mean negative log-likelihood per token).
label: core

section: 6 · perplexity, and why it depends on the tokenizer
text: Lower is better, and it is the training loss (cross entropy per token) read as a score on held-out text.
label: core
key: training cross entropy read as a score

section: 6 · perplexity, and why it depends on the tokenizer
text: The catch is N : it counts tokens, and different tokenizers cut the same text into different numbers of tokens.
label: core

section: 6 · perplexity, and why it depends on the tokenizer
text: The total log-probability of the text is comparable across models; dividing it by a model-specific token count is not.
label: core
key: total log-probability of a text is comparable

section: 6 · perplexity, and why it depends on the tokenizer

text: Information quantities Entropy H ( P ) = −Σ P log P (the average bits to encode samples of P with P 's own optimal code), cross entropy H ( P , Q ) = −Σ P log Q (with a code built for Q ) and their difference, the KL divergence D KL ( P ‖ Q ) = Σ P log( P / Q ) (the extra bits for the wrong code; asymmetric, no triangle inequality), are the root page's thread 1, "Everything is cross entropy", with its slider.
label: owned:models_and_training/topic_ml_fundamentals

text: On this page they appear as log-loss (section 3) and perplexity (section 6).
label: depth

text: Minimising cross entropy over Q is minimising KL, since H ( P ) is fixed; with one-hot labels H ( P ) = 0 and cross entropy = KL = the negative log-likelihood of the true class.
label: depth
